extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and scientifically literate readers interested in biogeography and paleontology
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for interpreting the fossil record and modern species distributions to evaluate descent with modification (biogeography and paleontology evidence). Focuses on expectations from an imperfect geological record, the role of barriers and migration, and the law of succession of types within areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection of the geological record
rubrics_metrics.description: The geological record is extremely imperfect and only a small portion of the globe has been geologically explored; only certain classes of organisms are largely preserved; the number of specimens and species preserved is negligible compared to the number of generations that have passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect continuous series of intermediate forms in the fossil record. Allow for long, blank intervals between formations, unequal durations of deposition, subsidence/elevation cycles that affect preservation, and regional incompleteness. Use this as a principal explanatory device for missing transitional links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of gaps between extinct and living forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Extinct forms are seldom directly intermediate between existing forms; they are often intermediate only by a long and circuitous course through many extinct and different forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether fossils contradict descent with modification, recognize that intermediacy will usually be partial or indirect; fossils may 'bring groups a little closer together' rather than neatly fill every gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate character of fauna from intermediate formations
rubrics_metrics.description: The fauna of any great geological period will be intermediate in general character between that which preceded and that which succeeded it, subject to allowances for extinction, immigration, and unequal time intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative position of formations and expected partial intermediacy to judge whether succession of forms supports descent. Example: fossils of the Devonian were seen as intermediate between Carboniferous and Silurian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close relationship of fossils from consecutive formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from remote formations; closely consecutive stages often show representative species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat strong similarity between consecutive-stage fossils as evidence of gradual change and lineage continuity rather than as evidence for immutability of species. Example: stages of the chalk formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative species and slow mutation
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to find, after geologically moderate intervals, closely allied or representative forms rather than every intermediate variety; these are the evidence of slow and scarcely sensible mutation of specific forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fossil sequences, look for representative, closely-allied forms across formations as the expected pattern of gradual change rather than continuous graded series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession of same types within same areas (law of succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a remarkable relationship in the same continent between extinct and living forms (the 'law of succession of types'): fossil mammals, birds, shells, etc., from a region are often closely allied to the living inhabitants of that same region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regional affinity between fossil and living taxa (e.g., South American fossil mammals related to modern South American types; New Zealand extinct birds related to living ones) as strong evidence for common descent and in favor of origin-with-migration rather than multiple independent creations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present distribution cannot be accounted for by physical conditions alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither similarity nor dissimilarity of inhabitants of various regions can be explained solely by climate and physical conditions — widely different faunas can exist under similar climates and closely related ones under different climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute major explanatory weight to historical factors (inheritance, migration, barriers, time) rather than just to present-day physical conditions when judging patterns of species distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of barriers to migration
rubrics_metrics.description: Barriers of any kind (oceans, isthmuses, mountain ranges, deserts, open sea with no islands) are closely related to differences between regional faunas and floras; barriers check migration and thus foster distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting distributional dissimilarities, evaluate the presence, nature and persistence of barriers historically and presently; absence of dispersal routes explains high regional distinctness (examples: Panama isthmus; Pacific islands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinity of productions of the same continent or sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Species in the same continent or sea show a general affinity: successive groups of specifically distinct yet closely related forms replace each other geographically, producing recognisable continental types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the pattern of related replacement along geographic gradients (e.g., north–south series of related species) as evidence of inherited regional lineages rather than convergent adaptation to similar climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-area origin and subsequent migration of species
rubrics_metrics.description: Each species was most probably produced in one area and subsequently migrated as far as its dispersal and subsistence permitted; cases of apparently disjunct ranges are exceptional and require historical explanation (migration, former continuity, climatic/geographical change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor explanations invoking single-origin plus migration over multiple independent origins; evaluate claimed exceptions by considering past connections, climatic changes, and means of dispersal. The simplicity of single-area origin is preferred as vera causa unless strong contrary evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of migration, climate and land-level changes, and occasional means in dispersal
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of dispersal include ordinary migration, changes of climate and levels of the land, and occasional or extraordinary means (including widespread dispersal during the Glacial period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explaining present and past distributions, consider a suite of dispersal mechanisms and historical events (e.g., glacial-period co-extensive dispersal) rather than relying on contemporary dispersal ability alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widely-ranging species are most variable and speciate most
rubrics_metrics.description: Widely-ranging species, abounding in individuals, vary most and have most frequently given rise to new species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing likely sources of new taxa and interpreting phylogeographic patterns, give weight to widespread, numerous species as probable ancestors of many descendant lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance, modification, and extinction dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant species of large groups tend to leave many modified descendants; less vigorous groups (inherited inferiority) tend to become extinct together and leave no modified offspring; extinction of whole groups may be slow due to survival in isolated refugia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differential success, competitive replacement, and refugial persistence to interpret patterns of diversification and the staggered disappearance of taxa in the fossil record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreversibility of extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a group has once wholly disappeared it does not reappear, because the generational link has been broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apparent reappearances skeptically and look for cases of mistaken identification, relict populations, or misinterpreted stratigraphy; extinction is effectively irreversible in lineage terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about 'higher' and 'lower' organisation judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalists have not defined satisfactorily what is meant by high and low forms; while recent victorious forms may be 'higher' in the sense of having advantages in the struggle for life, comparisons are ambiguous and difficult to test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic teleological rankings of taxa as an objective criterion; treat claims of progress with caution and seek explicit, testable measures rather than vague hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential embryological evidence for ancient conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agassiz's idea that ancient animals resemble to some extent the embryos of recent animals (geological succession parallel to embryological development) is plausible for subordinate, recently-branching groups and accords with natural selection, but remains far from proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider embryological similarity as a possible line of evidence for ancestral states, but require careful testing and recognize current limitations of proof; expect embryo conservation while adult forms diverge by later-acting variations.
